To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cytoplasmically derived factors can exert negative control of gene expression, that the cytoplasmic control is short-lived, and that the nucleus is required for the renewal of the control.
(1) the cytoplasm of mouse fibroblats suppresses the expression of the rat albumin gene, and that (2) this suppression is short-lived, lasting only about 48 h.
cytoplasm from mouse fibroblastic cells suppresses albumin gene expression in cybrids with hepatoma nuclei, but that the suppressive effect is not permanent and is lost by 48 hours after fusion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of cytoplasmic components in the control of gene regulation and expression in mammalian somatic cells.
the role of cytoplasmic components in the expression of the albumins genes and other genes of rat hepatoma cells.
the role of cytoplasmic regulation in the expression of the albumingene in mouse-fibroblast and rat-hepatoma cybrid cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the short-lived cytoplasm is not renewed in the cytoplasm of the cybrids.

the cytoplasm of the fibroblasts is capable of exerting a negative control on the expression of albumin genes in hepatoma cells, and that this control is exerted by a short-lived factor which is not present in the fibroblast nucleus.
the cytoplasmic hybridization experiments described here provide evidence that the cytoplasons of the fibroblasts contain a short-lived factor which suppresses albumin production by Fao cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cytoplasmic hybridization of mouse fibroblastic cells with rat hepatoma cells resulted in a transient inhibition of albumin production in the hybrids.
cytoplasm is not a static environment, but rather an active one that contains short-lived regulators of gene expression.
the cytoplasmic control of gene expression is not a permanent phenomenon but is a short-lived one, lasting for a few cell generations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of enucleation and fusion techniques to prepare modified cells for study of gene regulation is feasible, and that the use of cybrids is particularly advantageous for studying short-lived cytoplasmically controlled regulatory factors.
it is possible to study the effects of cytoplasmic gene regulators without the use of long term selection and without the possibility of chromosomal loss.
cytoplasm is not just an inert bag of organelles, but rather it contains a variety of short-lived regulatory proteins and RNAs which may be involved in the control of gene activity in eukaryotes.
